content: The primary data source for the HIV patient monitoring system is the facility-based HIV patient card, which contains the complete HIV-specific minimum dataset. This card may also be referred to as a patient record or file in some settings. It includes detailed information such as reproductive and family planning choices (including current pregnancy status), antenatal care (ANC) numbers, child vaccination records, sexually transmitted infection (STI) test results, nutritional support and infant-feeding practices (including breastfeeding status), and the status of HIV-exposed infants (including name, date of birth, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, HIV test type and results, final status, and unique ID if confirmed HIV-positive). The HIV patient card is divided into three sections. The front page summarizes the patient’s demographic, family, HIV care, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) information. The second section, the encounter page, records details of each clinical visit, with the first row representing the baseline visit. When the page is full, additional blank sheets can be attached. Health workers are expected to review and document the required information during each visit, using the provided code boxes as a guide. The third section focuses on patient education and counseling, including adherence support, which can be completed by the same health worker or a counselor/educator. It is essential to prioritize key points during each visit and document them clearly for follow-up purposes. The HIV patient card has undergone several revisions. Updates to the front of the card include recommendations for initiating the card at the point of entry, assigning unique IDs to all patients enrolling in HIV care (regardless of ART start date), and discontinuing its use for HIV-exposed infants before HIV infection confirmation. Other changes include updates to reflect differentiated care models, simplified family status information (with the addition of the date of death), inclusion of the date of the first HIV-positive test, and the addition of relevant chronic conditions, concomitant medications, and a tuberculosis (TB) status box. Third-line ART regimens and follow-up status date columns have also been added. Revisions to the encounter page include the addition of vaccination information to the pregnancy/reproductive health column, a new column for hepatitis status, and updates to terminology (e.g., treatment-limiting toxicities instead of potential side effects). The codes page has also been updated to reflect changes in pregnancy/reproductive health choices, family planning methods, comorbidities, TB status, and treatment-limiting toxicities. Vaccination and hepatitis information codes have been added. The ART register, which contains key information from the HIV patient card, is organized by the month and year the patient starts ART and tracks follow-up over time, including CD4 counts and viral load results. It is used to aggregate data for ART cohort and cross-sectional reports. WHO recommends maintaining ART registers at all treatment facilities, including antenatal care (ANC) and TB clinics, to facilitate data reconciliation and longitudinal follow-up of patient cohorts. The ART register has also been updated to align with the treat all approach, removing the pre-ART register and revising data elements such as baseline CD4 count, pregnancy/breastfeeding status, and TB preventive therapy. Routine viral load testing is recommended at six months after ART initiation, repeated at 12 months, and annually thereafter. CD4 monitoring can be discontinued if viral load is stable. Community-based patient monitoring tools are recommended under the differentiated care model, allowing stable patients on ART to access decentralized services and reducing the burden on clinical settings. Community health workers (CHWs) play a critical role in monitoring stable patients, distributing medications, providing psychosocial support, and linking patients to community-based support groups. The generic transfer form includes key details from the HIV patient card and a counter-referral section to notify the referring facility of a successful transfer. Monitoring and evaluation of HIV care programs rely on cross-sectional and cohort reports derived from the ART register. Cross-sectional reports provide a snapshot of patient data at a specific time, while cohort reports track outcomes for groups of patients who started ART during the same period. These reports are essential for identifying trends, addressing gaps in care, and improving program performance. Efforts to integrate HIV care with maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) services are critical for eliminating mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV. This includes lifelong ART for HIV-positive pregnant women, early infant diagnosis, and adherence to breastfeeding recommendations. Monitoring systems should capture the continuum of care for pregnant women living with HIV, from ART initiation to viral suppression, and integrate PMTCT and pediatric HIV services with MNCH care. Unique patient identifiers and integrated patient records are essential for accurate data management and continuity of care. Innovative approaches, such as single patient records and electronic medical record systems, are being adopted in various settings to improve data integration and patient management.
